I found the transition in the Results from Fig 1 to Fig 2 a bit hard to follow. I’d appreciate it
if the authors unpacked their findings related to these figures a bit more in the Results.
For example, the transition from the anterior/posterior hippocampal ROI effects and then
comparing hippocampus, entorhinal cortex, and the vmPFC is very abrupt.
Response to Reviewer 1, Comment 4:
We have added a new paragraph that smooths the transition between analyses focused on the
hippocampus and comparisons across regions (see Response to Reviewer 1, Comment 3
above). The new text clarifies the rationale for dissociating representations in the
hippocampus, entorhinal cortex, amygdala, and vmPFC.
Reviewer 1, Comment 5.1:
Somewhat linked to my first comment, I wasn’t satisfied with the justification of using a
computational model of cognitive map-like knowledge representations to model
hippocampal-entorhinal and mPFC data that wasn’t shown to represent map-like affective
knowledge. The authors could run a univariate or multivariate fMRI analysis of trajectories
between emotional concepts and events in the 2D multidimensional scaling projection of the
emotional concept data as a way to better justify their model-informed fMRI analyses.
Response to Reviewer 1, Comment 5.1:
Although it may not have been clear, our intention was to first demonstrate that information
about emotion concepts and valence-arousal dimensions was present in hippocampal-
prefrontal systems to justify the use of TEM. We took the hierarchical structure evident in
hippocampal decoders to suggest that representations in these regions could be map-like
(rather than just independent schema) and that they might resemble those learned by an agent
experiencing transitions between emotional events. We now make this strategy more explicit
in the introduction of the manuscript on lines 103-106.
“Given evidence of map-like representations in hippocampal-prefrontal systems, we
complement these analyses using a computational model of relational memory (the
Tolman-Eichenbaum Machine (Whittington et al., 2020); TEM) that formulates how
an agent might learn from event sequences to construct cognitive maps.”
That said, we could have provided stronger evidence of map-like representation based on
self-report data before moving on to computational approaches. Following the reviewer’s
suggestion, we have conducted a new analysis in which we 1) use multidimensional scaling
to transform category ratings into locations in a continuous, two-dimensional affective space,
and 2) decode fMRI signal acquired as participants watched cinematic movies to predict
trajectories in this two-dimensional space. As predicted, we found that hippocampal activity
contained more information about emotion categories than either neocortical region. Partially
consistent with our prediction, we found that vmPFC contained more information about the
two-dimensional affective space. Signals in entorhinal cortex did not robustly encode
emotion concepts or locations in the two-dimensional affective space. These findings more
strongly justify the use of TEM to characterize map-like coding of emotion concepts. Results
of this new analysis are included in Response to Reviewer 1, Comment 2.2 (Fig. R1) above.
Reviewer 1, Comment 5.2:
For example, it was unclear how the g parameter in the TEM relates to grid-like coding in
the fMRI data?
Response to Reviewer 1, Comment 5.2:
We now provide additional rationale explaining how activation in the population of g cells in
TEM relates to BOLD signal in vmPFC on lines 237-244.
“In contrast, activity in layer g resembles that of entorhinal cortex, with firing fields
that span the entire space (e.g., grid cell-like activity; Fig. 4c), providing an abstract
structural code that can be used for making inferences in any environment or in new
problems that have a similar relational structure. In this way, TEM formalizes how an
agent learns representations thought to be present in hippocampal-prefrontal systems.
This model allowed us to test whether hippocampal signals more accurately predict
the conjunction of concepts and their location in the affective space (activity in the p
layer), and whether vmPFC signals more accurately predict the relational structure of
affective space (activity in the g layer).”
Reviewer 1, Comment 6:
Given its important role in emotional memory and the authors’ previous work, I was
surprised that the authors don’t present results from a bilateral amygdala ROI as a way to
better distinguish the role of different regions in mapping different emotion concepts. The
amygdala probably plays an important role in most cognitive processes that they’re
interested in without having a strong association with cognitive maps. It would also further
strengthen their anterior versus posterior hippocampal axis data.
Response to Reviewer 1, Comment 6:
We agree that including an analysis of amygdala activity helps contextualize our findings.
Performing the same decoding analyses used to investigate signals in the hippocampus,
entorhinal cortex, and vmPFC, we found that amygdala activity predicted category ratings,
locations in affective space, and valence-arousal ratings to some degree (all > chance; Fig.
R2). However, amygdala decoders exhibited low levels of performance and did not encode
more information about emotion categories than locations in a two-dimensional affective
space (Δz = -0.0036, 95% bootstrap CI [-0.0102, 0.0033], d = -0.0195, p = .2213). Direct
comparisons with hippocampal decoders showed that the amygdala was less accurate at
predicting category ratings than the hippocampus, more so than for predicting valence-
arousal ratings (Δz = -0.0092, 95% bootstrap CI [-0.0037, -0.0149], d = -0.6004, p = .0146;
Fig. R3a).
Given prior evidence of strong anatomical and functional connectivity between the amygdala
and anterior hippocampus (Freelin et al., 2025; Poppenk et al., 2013), and some evidence that
the amygdala encodes abstract knowledge (Kumaran et al., 2012), we additionally compared
amygdala decoding performance with that of anterior and posterior hippocampus separately
(Fig. R3b). Amygdala responses did not predict category ratings as accurately as signals in
the posterior hippocampus (Δz = -0.0117, 95% bootstrap CI [-0.0063, -0.0171], d = -0.7850,
p = .0014), particularly relative to predicting binarized valence-arousal ratings (Δz = -0.0125,
95% bootstrap CI [-0.0077, -0.0172], d = -0.9538, p = .0017). By contrast, amygdala and
anterior hippocampus exhibited comparable levels of performance when decoding category
ratings (Δz = -0.0040, 95% bootstrap CI [-0.0015, -0.0095], d = -0.2660, p = .2286), with no
evidence of differences between regions (amygdala vs. anterior hippocampus) in decoding of
category vs. binarized valence-arousal variables (Δz = -0.0023, 95% bootstrap CI[-0.0024, -
0.0071], d = -0.1780, p = 0.4813). This pattern is consistent with prior evidence implicating
amygdala (Kong & Zweifel, 2021), anterior hippocampus and their interactions in
representing broad affective context, which may in turn support the enhancement of memory
for emotionally salient events (Freelin et al., 2025; Poppenk et al., 2013).
Figure R3. Decoding emotion category ratings, locations in affective space, and
binarized valence-arousal ratings from BOLD response patterns in hippocampal-
prefrontal systems and the amygdala. a Performance of decoding models trained to
predict emotion category ratings and locations in two-dimensional affective space from
BOLD signal in hippocampus, vmPFC, and amygdala. b Performance of decoding models
trained to predict emotion category and binarized valence-arousal ratings from BOLD
activity in anterior hippocampus, posterior hippocampus, and amygdala. In both panels, each
point represents the prediction-outcome correlation averaged across category rating items,
two-dimensional locations, or binarized valence-arousal items from a single subject (n = 29
independent subjects). Points from the same subjects are connected by gray lines, black lines
indicate the mean, and gray dashed lines represent chance.
These new findings have been incorporated into the results section of the manuscript on lines
167-182 and in revised figures 2 and 3.
Minor comments
Reviewer 1, Comment 7:
It would be helpful to separate the Results and Discussion sections by giving them their own
headings.
Response to Reviewer 1, Comment 7:
We have added descriptive subheadings in the Results section and following the journal
formatting guideline, we did not provide subheadings in the Discussion section, although we
are open to this possibility if the journal is willing to accommodate.
Reviewer 1, Comment 8:
In the Discussion, the authors say previous abstract cognitive map work relies on an
“Impoverished sensory environment,” while the authors’ “use of naturalistic movie stimuli
offers a more ecologically valid window into how hippocampal-prefrontal systems process
dynamic, rich, emotional experiences”. However, I fail to see how interactive tasks like
Tavares et al., 2015 Neuron or Park et al., 2021, Neuron, where participants learn social
hierarchies with natural dimensions like popularity, power, or competence are any less
interactive than the emotional concepts in this task. I recommend removing that sentence in the Discussion.
Response to Reviewer 1, Comment 8:
This comment in the discussion section was intended to highlight that most work in this space
(Park et al 2021 and Tavares et al 2015 included) use relatively simplified stimuli. Static
images of faces and narrative text are far from the sensory inputs that humans learn about
outside of the scanning environment. We agree that other tasks are more naturalistic to the
extent that they involve active navigation, but issues regarding the complexity of sensory
inputs remain. We have revised the discussion to note this distinction in the revision on lines
371-375.
“Previous investigations have characterized brain responses to less complex stimuli
(Constantinescu et al., 2016; Park et al., 2021; Viganò et al., 2021), such as static
images or text-based narratives. Although our experimental paradigm was not
interactive, our use of naturalistic movies offers a more ecologically valid window
into how hippocampal-prefrontal systems process dynamic, rich, emotional
experiences.”
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Reviewer 2, Comment 1:
The authors report results from an fMRI study in which participants (N = 29) viewed
emotionally evocative film clips. The fMRI results show that activity in hippocampus and
prefrontal cortex predict self-reported emotion across schematically distinct videos.
Specifically, the results suggest that the hippocampus represents a hierarchy of emotion
concepts (with greater granularity in the posterior hippocampus), and that the ventromedial
prefrontal cortex represents large-scale structural abstractions. The methods seem sound and
sophisticated, including interesting simulations using the Tolman-Eichenbaum machine
applied to a 2D emotional space. The manuscript is well written and the results are exciting.
Furthermore, the manuscript bridges two big topics: emotional processing and spatial
navigation / cognitive maps, and it will thus be of interest to a large audience.
My specific comments are as follows:
- Line 114: It would be helpful for the reader to first learn more about the task and behavior
of participants before the fMRI results are presented. Currently, it's hard to follow the fMRI
results without knowing what the task, stimuli, or participant behavior looked like. A new,
separate figure on these aspects would be very helpful. This should also include how well the
different emotions and the valence-arousal space was sampled.
Response to Reviewer 2, Comment 1:
We thank the reviewer for this helpful suggestion. We have added a new figure (Fig. R4; now
Fig. 1 in the main text) that illustrates the stimuli, fMRI and behavioral data, including the
coverage of emotion categories and the valence-arousal space in the self-report ratings.
Figure R4. Experimental paradigm and behavior. a participants (n = 29) watched over 2.5 h
of 14 brief cinematic videos while BOLD signal was measured with fMRI over the course of 4
scanning sessions. The video stimuli were additionally rated by an independent group of 44
subjects. Here we examine continuous ratings of 13 emotion categories, 2 measures of valence,
and 2 measures of arousal. b Hexagonal binned plot of self-report data. Each hexagon
represents a region of a two-dimensional space defined by ratings of valence (x-axis) and
arousal (y-axis) across films. Bins are colored to indicate the category with the highest rating
across time points falling in that region. Blank areas indicate bins without observations in the
corresponding valence-arousal range. Hexagonal binned plots for each individual emotion
category are shown in Supplementary Fig. 1.
Reviewer 2, Comment 2:
- Line 166: I'm confused about the statement that "valence-arousal dimensions were more
accurately decoded in vmPFC and entorhinal cortex compared to the hippocampus." In Fig.
2b, the blue dots for entorhinal cortex are at lower values than the blue dots for
hippocampus, so why do the authors say that valence-arousal dimensions are more
accurately decoded in entorhinal cortex?
Response to Reviewer 2, Comment 2:
The sentence in question originally referred to a contrast in which the entorhinal cortex and
vmPFC were averaged together as a neocortical group and compared against the
hippocampus ((entorhinal cortex + vmPFC)/2 - hippocampus). We included this contrast only
for the valence-arousal decoding analysis as an initial test of our hypothesis that neocortical
regions implicated in structural abstraction (vmPFC and entorhinal cortex) would, as a group,
more accurately track valence-arousal dimensions compared to the hippocampus. The
original phrasing was not clear and could be read as referring to the individual entorhinal
cortex results. Indeed, the more accurate valence-arousal decoding in the neocortical group
was driven by the vmPFC (Δz = 0.0398, 95% bootstrap CI [0.0308, 0.0489], d = 1.5951, p
< .0001), whereas absolute valence-arousal decoding performance in the entorhinal cortex
was lower than in the hippocampus (Δz = -0.0127, 95% bootstrap CI [-0.0218, -0.0033], d = -
0.504, p = .0040). However, the key point was the relative difference between category and
valence-arousal; the category-dimension gap was larger in the hippocampus than in the
entorhinal cortex or vmPFC. This interaction effect indicates that hippocampus is more
category-focused, and neocortical areas preserved relatively more information about affective
dimensions.
In the revised manuscript, we present a new analysis decoding locations in a two-dimensional
affective space derived from multidimensional scaling of category ratings as a more direct
measure of the relational space, as opposed to decoding self-reported valence and arousal.
We now report results separately for vmPFC and entorhinal cortex on lines XXXXX of the
manuscript and it was also included in Response to Reviewer 1, Comment 2.2 (Fig. R1)
above.
Reviewer 2, Comment 3:
- Line 62: The statement "suggesting that these variables are the most fundamental property
of the mind" seems too strong - I would suggest toning this down.
Response to Reviewer 2, Comment 3:
We agree—this may not be a generally accepted interpretation, nor is it a view that we
strongly hold. We have toned this language down to note that it is a perspective held by some
theorists.
Reviewer 2, Comment 4:
- Line 150: Liu et al., Current Biology, 2023 ("Multi-scale goal distance representations in
human hippocampus during virtual spatial navigation") is also relevant with regard to more
rapid changes in the posterior human hippocampus.
Response to Reviewer 2, Comment 4:
This study is indeed relevant to the present work. We now include a reference to this work on
lines 151-155.
“Central to accounts of memory, navigation, and emotion processing (Fanselow &
Dong, 2010), the hippocampal long axis is characterized by gradients in connectivity,
gene expression (Vogel et al., 2020), neural timescale (Liu et al., 2023), and
behavioral specialization (Collin et al., 2015; Komorowski et al., 2013). Particularly
relevant for the representation of emotion knowledge are observations that
hippocampal activity represents event sequences at multiple timescales, with more
rapid changes coded in more posterior portions of the hippocampus (Collin et al.,
2015; Liu et al., 2023).”
Reviewer 2, Comment 5:
- The authors should state that fMRI cannot resolve a lot of neural processes that happen at
rapid time scales and at the cellular level (due to its low temporal and spatial resolution), so
there may be many neural processes of emotional processing that this study may have missed.
This limitation (and also other limitations) should be stated clearly.
Response to Reviewer 2, Comment 5:
We have included a discussion of limitations on lines 403-417.
“Several limitations constrain the interpretation of our findings. Our focus on
dimensions of valence and arousal necessarily oversimplifies emotional experience,
which can be organized by far more than two dimensions (Cowen et al., 2019;
Fontaine et al., 2007). Emotion knowledge may be organized in low-dimensional
embeddings of other variables, such as effort, certainty, and situational control.
Additionally, the spatiotemporal resolution of fMRI precludes measurement of neural
dynamics and phase codes thought to support navigation (Burgess & O’Keefe, 2011;
Lisman & Jensen, 2013). To the extent that neural mechanisms are shared across
species, future research using high-density neuronal recordings in rodents (Wen et al.,
2024; Zutshi et al., 2025) and human intracranial electrophysiology (Qasim et al.,
2021) will be critical for testing whether navigating affective spaces involves
computations similar to those used for spatial navigation. Further, TEM is not the
only model of hippocampal computations. Alternative models grounded in
reinforcement learning (Stachenfeld et al., 2017) may offer complementary insights,
particularly for studying emotion concepts, which inherently encode value and
motivational relevance. This framework aligns with evidence suggesting the role of
the anterior hippocampus and vmPFC in motivation and goal-directed behavior (Gazit
et al., 2020; Strange et al., 2014; Viard et al., 2011). Future research should examine
whether models of reinforcement learning can better predict hippocampal-prefrontal
representations of emotion concepts.”
Reviewer 2, Comment 6:
- Were there differences between medial and lateral entorhinal cortex?
Response to Reviewer 2, Comment 6:
We did not previously analyze fMRI signal in lateral and medial entorhinal cortex separately,
because we had expected entorhinal cortex as a whole to contain more information about
affective space or valence-arousal ratings. Because we did not find signals related to these
variables, we did not probe further subdivisions to avoid over-interpreting noise or increasing
the risk of false positives. Had we found strong mappings between entorhinal cortex
responses and emotion concepts or affective space, we could have attempted to localize
concepts to lateral entorhinal cortex and the affective space to medial entorhinal cortex, as
predicted by our account.
Based on the reviewer’s suggestion, we conducted separate decoding analyses within the
posteromedial and anterolateral entorhinal cortex using masks from Maass et al. (2015).
Using these masks, we did not observe differences between entorhinal subregions, nor
between either subregion and the entorhinal cortex as a whole (Figs. R5 and R6).
Figure R5. Performance of decoding models trained to predict emotion category and
valence-arousal rating in subregions of the entorhinal cortex. Performance of decoding
models trained to predict emotion category ratings (orange circles) and valence-arousal ratings
(blue circles) from BOLD signal in whole, anterolateral, and posteromedial entorhinal cortex.
Each point represents the prediction-outcome correlation averaged across category rating
items or two-dimensional locations from a single subject (n = 29 independent subjects). Points
from the same subjects are connected by gray lines, black lines indicate the mean, and gray
dashed lines represent chance.
Figure R6. Performance of decoding models trained to predict activity of p and g cells
from BOLD activity in subregions of the entorhinal cortex. Each point represents the
prediction-outcome correlation averaged across units at each scale from one subject (n = 29
independent subjects). Horizontal black lines indicate the group average, connected gray
lines indicate performance for one subject, and the horizontal dashed line indicates chance.
TEM = Tolman Eichenbaum Machine.
One might expect differences between posteromedial and anterolateral entorhinal cortex,
suggested as the human homologues of the rodent medial and lateral entorhinal cortex (Maass
et al., 2015; Navarro Schröder et al., 2015). However, several factors may have limited our
ability to detect such differences here. First, susceptibility artifacts are particularly severe in
the entorhinal cortex, which can lead to signal loss and distortion (Olman et al., 2009),
though our inspection of the variation of mean signal across subjects did not reveal unusual
instability or obvious signal dropout within this region (see Fig. R7). Second, segmenting
posteromedial and anterolateral entorhinal cortex is challenging and typically requires manual
segmentation of high-resolution images at 7T (Maass et al., 2015; Navarro Schröder et al.,
2015). These constraints, along with the generally lower decoding performance we observed
in the entorhinal cortex, may have obscured functional distinctions between posteromedial
and anterolateral entorhinal cortex in our analysis. Alternatively, it may be the case that the
entorhinal cortex plays a different role in organizing knowledge about emotions and space.
Figure R7. fMRI signal across subjects. For each subject, voxelwise signal intensity maps
were created by averaging preprocessed BOLD timeseries across all video viewing sessions.
Parametric maps show the group mean of signal intensity divided by the standard deviation
across subjects (i.e., Cohen’s d; n = 29 independent subjects). The colorbar indicates the
average signal intensity, with darker colors indicating values below average and warmer
colors indicating greater signal intensity. Note that preprocessing involved scaling the
timeseries relative to the grand mean and accounting for confounds. Note the lack of spatial
distortions or dropout in the anterior temporal lobe.
Reviewer 2, Comment 7:
- Line 351: Given the findings of the study, I was surprised that the authors used the term
"map-like representations of emotion concepts" when summarizing them - wouldn't "graph-
like representations" (or similar) be a better fit to the observations? Overall, the Conclusions
paragraph from line 351 to 359 felt somewhat disconnected from the actual observations of
the study.
Response to Reviewer 2, Comment 7:
We agree that relations among emotion concepts can be described in a graph-like way, and
indeed our simulation with TEM used both a discrete environment and action space.
However, we used the term “map-like” following the idea that cognitive maps in
hippocampal-prefrontal systems, for spatial and non-spatial problems, can be constructed
from statistical regularities in the transitions between discrete states (Behrens et al., 2018). In
short, we use the term “map-like” to refer to both relational maps and continuous maps. Our
findings provide evidence for both types of representations. We now clarify this point in the
Discussion section of the manuscript on lines 380-390.
“Our computational modeling results suggest that map-like representations in
hippocampal-prefrontal systems could result from learning the statistical regularities
of event transitions. By recasting continuous navigation as the problem of learning
transitions in a discrete state space, the same hippocampal-prefrontal representations
can be used to accomplish a variety of tasks, whether conceived as learning linkages
on a graph or directions in a two-dimensional Euclidean map (Behrens et al., 2018).
Our fMRI results are consistent with both conceptions of a cognitive map, as we
found hippocampal-prefrontal activity predicted both locations in a two continuous
affective space and activity in TEM—a model trained to perform structural
abstraction through learning transitions between discrete states. Whether graph-like
and map-like representations result from sequential stages of abstraction or
qualitatively distinct processes remains an open question for future research.”

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:

I still worry that readers will think their classifier analysis would find nonzero correlations everywhere in the brain, independent of whether the regions are involved in affective processing. For their supplemental results section, I encourage the authors to run a whole-brain searchlight analysis to show that at least some brain regions exhibit nonzero correlations for emotion category and valence/arousal.

The "general relational structure" in vmPFC they mention would be thought of as cognitive map-like by many investigators.
It'd be helpful to unpack these theoretical differences a bit more in the manuscript.

peer_review_rounds.author_response:
Response to Editors and Reviewers
We thank the reviewers for their thoughtful and constructive feedback on the manuscript. We
have 1) included the results of whole-brain searchlight analyses, and 2) clarified the distinct
formats of map-like representations in the hippocampal-prefrontal systems. Below we
provide a point-by-point response to both comments raised during review. Reviewer
comments are provided in italics, and our responses are presented in normal font. Quotations
from the revised manuscript are provided in indented blocks of text.
Reviewer 1, Comment 1:
I commend the authors for the substantial analyses and revisions they've made in response to
my concerns. Prior to publication at Nature Communications, I have two minor suggestions
that would make their findings more straightforward to interpret.
-I appreciate the authors' response to my third comment about the performance of individual
decoders versus chance. I still worry that readers will think their classifier analysis would
find nonzero correlations everywhere in the brain, independent of whether the regions are
involved in affective processing. For their supplemental results section, I encourage the
authors to run a whole-brain searchlight analysis to show that at least some brain regions
exhibit nonzero correlations for emotion category and valence/arousal.
Response to Reviewer 1, Comment 1:
We thank the reviewer for their positive evaluation of our revision and for the helpful
suggestions to further clarify our findings. We conducted a whole-brain searchlight analysis
and visualized the variation of effect sizes of decoding performance (Fig. R1 and
Supplementary Fig. 10). Cohen’s d ranged from 0 to 6.01 for the performance of decoders
trained to predict emotion category ratings, and from -0.19 to 2.98 for valence-arousal
decoding. As can be seen in the figure, most information about these variables was present in
response patterns in medial prefrontal cortex, precuneus, parietal cortex, and temporal cortex.
These structures are frequently found to respond to emotion manipulations (Lindquist et al.,
2012) and contain information about emotion categories (see Satpute & Lindquist, 2019 for
review of decoding studies). We now include the results of this searchlight analysis in the
supplemental materials to illustrate variability in the amount of emotion-related information
in fMRI signal.
We stress that our key inferences stem from hypothesis-driven region-of-interest analyses
that directly compare decoding performance between regions, rather than testing each
decoder against chance. We prefer this approach because subthreshold activity can carry
meaningful information and regional differences can reflect quantitative rather than
qualitative distinctions (Etzel et al., 2013; Henson, 2006). Moreover, because specific
emotional states are characterized by information contained in spatially distributed yet
overlapping response patterns, observations from searchlight analyses may miss out on
information related to processes that unfold at larger spatial scales (Etzel et al., 2013; Kragel
et al., 2018). Based on these considerations, observing widespread and variable decoding
performance above chance across the brain is expected and complements our main results
showing how different regions represent emotion-related variables.
Figure R1. Voxelwise effect sizes of decoding performance. Maps reflect effect sizes of
the performance of decoders trained to predict (a) emotion categories and (b) valence-arousal
from searchlight spheres (radius = 4 voxels). The colorbar indicates Cohen’s d of Fisher-z
transformed prediction-outcome correlations across subjects (n = 29 independent subjects).
Reviewer 1, Comment 2:
-I'd recommend revising the manuscript one more time to further distinguish map-like
representations of hierarchically organized structure versus 2D representations of affective
space. At first glance, it's unclear why one of the aforementioned representations would be
more 'map-like' than the other since there are plenty of studies that study 2D relational
representations in the hippocampus and elsewhere that are interpreted as cognitive maps.
For instance, in their response the authors state "These results are consistent with the idea
that the hippocampus represents emotion concepts embedded in a two-dimensional map,
whereas vmPFC represents a general relational structure that could be used to organize
emotions and other concepts". The "general relational structure" in vmPFC they mention
would be thought of as cognitive map-like by many investigators. It'd be helpful to unpack
these theoretical differences a bit more in the manuscript.
Response to Reviewer 1, Comment 2:
We have revised the introduction to make it clear that both hippocampus and vmPFC exhibit
map-like representations but in different formats on lines 87-94:
“To build a map of the environment, neural populations in the hippocampus bind
together highly processed sensory inputs with their positions in relational space,
forming conjunctive codes of concepts that jointly represent what is experienced and
where it lies within a structured map (Manns & Eichenbaum, 2006). Based on the
coactivation of hippocampal inputs, neural populations in the entorhinal cortex
(Hafting et al., 2005) and ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC) learn relations
among concepts using a grid-like code (Constantinescu et al., 2016; Nitsch et al.,
2024; Park et al., 2021; Viganò et al., 2023, 2021). This format abstracts away from
the content of experiences to define a relational structure which can be used to guide
decision making and navigate affective experiences.”
And on lines 99-106:
“Here we evaluate the proposal (Ma et al., 2025) that hippocampal-prefrontal systems
represent emotion concepts in a cognitive map. In this account, entorhinal and
ventromedial prefrontal cortex learn a general relational structure that can be used to
predict the valence and arousal of upcoming events. Through associative learning, the
hippocampus binds this information with highly processed sensory inputs to link
specific emotion concepts with locations in valence-arousal space. Thus, although
both sets of regions can be considered to have map-like properties, the hippocampus
should uniquely represent emotion concepts embedded in a two-dimensional affective
space. We test this account by analyzing fMRI signals...”
We have also revised the discussion to clarify that our findings in vmPFC can be considered
map-like in certain respects on lines 363-367:
“Considered alongside evidence that vmPFC and other nodes of the default network
exhibit grid-like activity during tasks from multiple domains (Bao et al., 2019;
Constantinescu et al., 2016; Park et al., 2021), these findings suggest that similar
neural mechanisms may be involved for reward-based decision making (Grabenhorst
& Rolls, 2011), social inferences (Lockwood et al., 2024), and reporting emotional
experience (Čeko et al., 2022)—all of which involve relational processing and could
be solved using map-based strategies (Kaplan et al., 2017).

review_generation.input:
You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

Emotional experiences involve more than bodily reactions and momentary feelings—they depend on knowledge about the world that spans contexts and time. Although it is well established that individuals conceptualize emotions using a low-dimensional space organized by valence and arousal, the neural mechanisms giving rise to this configuration remain unclear. Here, we examine whether hippocampal-prefrontal circuits—neural structures implicated in forming cognitive maps—also support the structural abstraction of emotional experiences. Using functional MRI data collected as participants viewed emotionally evocative film clips, we find that hippocampal activity represents emotion concepts in a structured hierarchy, whereas ventromedial prefrontal cortex more accurately tracks locations in a two-dimensional affective space. Computational modeling reveals that hippocampal-prefrontal responses to films can be predicted based on the statistical regularities of emotion transitions across multiple temporal scales. These findings demonstrate that hippocampal-prefrontal systems represent emotion concepts in a map-like way at multiple levels of abstraction, offering insight into how the brain organizes emotion knowledge.

---

## Introduction

Our experience of emotions is more than just momentary reactions to the world and accompanying feelings. Humans rely on emotion concepts—knowledge that helps us categorize, communicate, and make sense of emotional events in our lives. Some emotional knowledge is grounded in the particulars of individual episodes, such as the adorable features of a specific childhood pet or the growl of an aggressive neighborhood dog. Other knowledge concerns properties of events that generalize across episodes, like an opportunity for a reward or the presence of a threat. Even though emotional events can differ widely in what we see, hear, think, or feel, we learn to abstract them into distinct categories of variable yet related instances.

Behavioral evidence demonstrates that humans compress information about complex emotional episodes into a low-dimensional affective space1–4. When individuals judge the meaning of words5,6, emotions conveyed by others7, predict how others are likely to feel in a given situation8, or self-report on their own experience9, their ratings primarily vary along dimensions of valence and arousal, evidence taken by some to suggest that these variables are among the most fundamental properties of the mind3. Based on these observations, it has been suggested that humans represent the structure of affect in a map-like way3,5 using dimensions of valence and arousal as the organizing axes. If represented in such a format, emotion concepts would be positioned at specific locations in a relational network, much like landmarks are placed on a Cartesian map. With experience, individuals would learn the structure of affective space, enabling them to predict transitions from one experience to the next (e.g., the tendency to shift from a state of anxiety to fear as a threat becomes more proximal10) and to make decisions based on the anticipated consequences of actions11.

Neuroscience research has begun to characterize how the brain represents knowledge about emotional events. Work in nonhuman animals12–16 and human neuroimaging studies17–21 has identified functionally dissociable systems involved in valence and arousal processing. Neuroimaging has revealed that different categories of emotional events are differentiated by patterns of activity that are distributed across subcortical and cortical brain networks22–24, with the content represented varying across regions. Responses to emotional situations range from more situation-dependent activity in sensory cortices25–28 and more general category representations in transmodal cortical areas29,30. Together, these studies show that the brain represents emotional events using multiple systems in parallel, and that information processing occurs in a hierarchical fashion.

Although it is well-established that multiple aspects of emotional events are reflected across brain systems, it remains unclear how emotionally relevant signals are transformed into low-dimensional affective spaces. One possibility is that memory systems necessary for organizing knowledge across domains are involved in mapping relationships between emotion events. Evidence suggests that the hippocampal formation—known for its involvement in spatial navigation31, memory32, and emotion33–35—represents knowledge in a map-like way36–40. To build a map of the environment, neural populations in the hippocampus bind together highly processed sensory inputs with their positions in relational space, forming conjunctive codes of concepts that jointly represent what is experienced and where it lies within a structured map41. Based on the coactivation of hippocampal inputs, neural populations in the entorhinal cortex42 and ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC) learn relations among concepts using a grid-like code36–40. This format abstracts away from the content of experiences to define a relational structure which can be used to guide decision making and navigation. If similar mechanisms are used to construct maps of emotion concepts43, then knowledge about distinct sets of emotional experiences should be encoded in patterns of hippocampal activity, whereas the spatial bases that define affective space (i.e., grid-like codes that span dimensions of valence and arousal) should be present in entorhinal cortex and vmPFC44.

In this work, we evaluate the proposal43 that hippocampal-prefrontal systems represent emotion concepts in a cognitive map. In this account, entorhinal and ventromedial prefrontal cortex learn a general relational structure that can be used to predict the valence and arousal of upcoming events. Through associative learning, the hippocampus binds this information with highly processed sensory inputs to link specific emotion concepts with locations in valence-arousal space. Thus, although both sets of regions can be considered to have map-like properties, the hippocampus uniquely represents emotion concepts embedded in a two-dimensional affective space. We test this account by analyzing fMRI signals acquired as human participants watched a series of cinematic videos (sampled from the Emo-FilM dataset45, Fig. 1). As information about prototypical emotional events is typically accessible to consciousness, we first probe whether self-report measures of emotional experience can be decoded from patterns of hippocampal-prefrontal activity, and whether representations of emotion categories are distinct from a two-dimensional representation of affective space. Finding evidence of map-like representations in hippocampal-prefrontal systems, we complement these analyses using a computational model of relational memory (the Tolman-Eichenbaum Machine46, TEM) that formulates how an agent might learn from event sequences to construct cognitive maps. We train artificial agents to learn the regularities of emotion-laden environments by binding sensory representations with structural knowledge about the world. After training, we show that patterns of BOLD time-series in hippocampal-prefrontal systems covary with internal representations in computational agents, and are associated with self-reported emotion. These experiments reveal that hippocampal-prefrontal systems represent emotion concepts in a map-like way, providing a neurocomputational explanation of how humans organize abstract emotion knowledge.

## Results

The hippocampus represents multiple emotion concepts in a hierarchically organized structure

We first evaluated whether hippocampal activity represents multiple emotion concepts in a format that is not merely based on variation in affect. To this end, we trained multivariate decoders (Supplementary Fig. 2) that map patterns of hippocampal fMRI time series (9538 measurements in 1816 voxels, per participant on average) onto either multivariate emotion category ratings, or locations in a two-dimensional space derived from multidimensional scaling of emotion category ratings (hereafter referred to as affective space, see Supplementary Fig. 3). Models were trained using data acquired from multiple film stimuli and evaluated by testing them on independent stimuli (leave-one-film-out cross-validation, 13 films total for each of n = 29 participants) and comparing the readout of category and affective space decoders (see “Methods”). This analysis revealed that category ratings were more accurately decoded (z = 0.0525, 95% bootstrap CI [0.0454, 0.0592]) than locations in affective space (z = 0.0428, 95% bootstrap CI [0.0347, 0.0505]; Δz = 0.0097, 95% bootstrap CI [0.0025, 0.0169], d = 0.4946, p < .001; see Supplementary Figs. 4, 5 for contributions of individual voxels). Together, these results are consistent with the proposal that the hippocampus encodes multiple emotion concepts in a format that is not reducible to a two-dimensional representation of affect.

Because the hippocampus represents event sequences in a hierarchical manner47–49, we expected that hippocampal responses to concepts that tend to occur in temporal proximity (e.g., disgust, anger, and guilt or anxiety, fear, and surprise) would be more similar to one another48, reflecting the graded similarity structure typically observed in ratings of emotion terms5,50,51 as opposed to a simple structure in which emotion concepts are independent. We assessed whether this was the case by analyzing the outputs of hippocampal decoders using agglomerative clustering. For each participant, we computed the similarity of model predictions over time to produce a conceptual similarity matrix (Supplementary Fig. 6). We modeled the similarity structure in two ways: with a model that estimated temporal similarity by averaging across concepts of the same valence (referred to as the valence model), and with another model that estimated temporal similarity for all pairs of concepts (the full model; Fig. 2c). To estimate model generalizability, we performed a leave-one-participant-out procedure in which temporal correlations were averaged across all but one participant and compared to the similarity structure of the held-out participant. This generalization test revealed that the correspondence across participants in the fully specified model (Spearman’s r = .978, SD = .007, 95% bootstrap CI [.975, 0.980], p < .001) was greater than that of the valence only model (Spearman’s r = .842, SD = .013, 95% bootstrap CI [.838, .847], p < .001; Fig. 2d), and that a substantial portion of variance across participants remained after accounting for valence (Spearman’s r = .486, SD = .014, 95% bootstrap CI [.481, .491], p < .001). These results suggest that the hippocampus does not represent emotion concepts independently, but as a hierarchy that is stable across participants (Fig. 2b) and captures relationships between emotions primarily along a dimension of valence.

Central to accounts of memory, navigation, and emotion processing52, the hippocampal long axis is characterized by gradients in connectivity, gene expression53, neural timescale54, and behavioral specialization55,56. Particularly relevant for the representation of emotion knowledge are observations that hippocampal activity represents event sequences at multiple timescales, with more rapid changes coded in more posterior portions of the hippocampus54,56. Such variation leads to the prediction that fine-grained distinctions between emotional events should be captured by activity in posterior hippocampus, whereas more general distinctions that take place over longer timescales should be represented in more anterior portions of the hippocampus. To examine variation in emotion representation along the hippocampal long axis, we trained multivariate decoders to predict variation in fine-grained (e.g., fear, anger, pride, joy or surprise) and broad emotion concepts (e.g., good, or activated) using signals either in the posterior or anterior hippocampus (based on a segmentation at the plane y = −21 in MNI space). Model comparisons revealed that decoding performance depended on both hippocampal portion and representational scale (Δz = 0.0101, 95% bootstrap CI [0.0054, 0.0149], d = 0.7791, p = .003, Fig. 2a), with greater decoding performance in posterior hippocampus as emotion granularity increased (see Supplementary Fig. 8 for performance on all ratings).

Complementing observations that knowledge from multiple domains is hierarchically organized in the hippocampus, evidence shows that the amygdala encodes some forms of abstract relationships, albeit in a different format than the hippocampus57. To assess whether this was the case for emotion concepts in the present study, we trained a new set of decoders on amygdala responses and compared their performance to that of those trained on signals in anterior and posterior hippocampus. We found amygdala responses did not predict category ratings as accurately as signals in posterior hippocampus (Δz = −0.0117, 95% bootstrap CI [−0.0063, −0.0171], d = −0.7850, p = .001), particularly when compared to predictions of binarized valence-arousal ratings (Δz = −0.0125, 95% bootstrap CI [−0.0077, −0.0172], d = −0.9538, p = .002). By contrast, amygdala decoders performed comparably to anterior hippocampal decoders (category ratings: Δz = −0.0040, 95% bootstrap CI [−0.0095, 0.0015], d = −0.2660, p = .229; region × target variable interaction: Δz = −0.0023, 95% bootstrap CI [−0.0071, 0.0024], d = −0.1780, p = 0.481; Fig. 2a). These results are broadly consistent with recent findings showing that the hippocampus and amygdala differ in their representations of abstract social relationships57,58, yet suggest that posterior hippocampus may be particularly important for organizing more fine-grained emotion knowledge.

Ventromedial prefrontal cortex represents trajectories in a two-dimensional affective space

We found that hippocampal BOLD signals contained information about emotion concepts, and to a lesser degree, information about trajectories in affective space. These observations suggest the hippocampus could play an important role in mapping emotion concepts—conveying information to the entorhinal cortex or vmPFC to construct an abstract, two-dimensional space36–40. If this is the case, then decoders trained on signals from these neocortical regions should predict trajectories in affective space more accurately than emotion category ratings. Alternatively, we may have observed better hippocampal prediction of category ratings because they were driven by particularly salient events, or because they occurred at time scales that are more easily captured by fMRI. In such cases, decoding performance should be higher for category ratings than trajectories in affective space, regardless of the neural origin of BOLD signals being decoded. Therefore, to dissociate representations across regions, we compared decoders trained to predict emotion category ratings and affective space using signals acquired in the hippocampus, entorhinal cortex, vmPFC, and the amygdala.

Consistent with a map-like representation, we found that signals from vmPFC predicted locations in affective space (z = 0.0956, 95% bootstrap CI [0.0831, 0.1076]) more accurately than emotion category ratings (z = 0.0838, 95% bootstrap CI [0.0777, 0.0902]; Δz = 0.0118, 95% bootstrap CI [0.0047, 0.0191], d = 0.0118, p = .020), similar to observations from studies examining decision-making about abstract social relationships58. This difference substantiated a double dissociation, such that the hippocampus contained more information about emotion category ratings whereas vmPFC better captured information about trajectories in affective space (Δz = 0.0215, 95% bootstrap CI [0.0134, 0.0297], d = 0.9566, p = .001; Fig. 3c). By contrast, activity in the entorhinal cortex and amygdala predicted the two target variables with comparable accuracy (entorhinal cortex: Δz = −0.0004, 95% bootstrap CI [−0.0071, 0.0067], d = −0.0195, p = .918; amygdala: Δz = −0.0036, 95% bootstrap CI [−0.0102, 0.0033], d = −0.0195, p = .221). Together, these results show that multiple regions carry information about emotion concepts (see Supplementary Fig. 9 for region-wise effect sizes and Supplementary Fig. 10 for results from less constrained searchlight mapping), and that the vmPFC contained more information about affective trajectories.

Of structures involved in relational and affective processing, several are known to encode independent dimensions of valence and arousal59–63 in addition to integrated, map-like representations. We therefore tested whether direct coding of each affective dimension measured in self-report could be decoded from BOLD signals acquired during film viewing using the same approach used to decode trajectories in affective space. Decoding continuous self-report ratings of valence and arousal produced similar results to affective space decoding, with the exception that readouts in vmPFC were not better predictors of valence and arousal than emotion category ratings (Supplementary Table 1 and Supplementary Figs. 11–14). These data suggest that vmPFC contains more integrated representations of affect compared to simple coding of independent affective dimensions.

Structural abstraction of emotion knowledge in hippocampal-prefrontal systems

The results of multivariate decoding experiments indicated that hippocampal-prefrontal systems represent emotion concepts in ways that resemble a cognitive map. Hippocampal activity carried more information about emotion category ratings while preserving their similarity structure, reflecting a hierarchical organization. The vmPFC more accurately tracked trajectories in affective space, suggestive of a low-dimensional relational code. This dissociation of function aligns with theoretical accounts suggesting that hippocampal binding of information about “what” occurs during an event and “where” it occurs in space and time could explain the formation of cognitive maps64,65. To more explicitly probe the representational format of emotion concepts in hippocampal-prefrontal systems, we simulated concept formation using TEM46, a computational model of relational memory (Fig. 4).

In learning to map the environment, TEM factorizes sensory observations into two separate bases—one that represents the contents of experience and another that represents relationships between experiences—and binds them together into a conjunctive code. This conjunction is represented in layer p, which is used to make predictions about upcoming sensory observations and locations in layer g. Activity in layer p resembles hippocampal population activity that encodes “what” is located “where” in an environment, with localized firing fields for specific concepts (Fig. 4c). In contrast, activity in layer g resembles that of entorhinal cortex, with firing fields that span the entire space (e.g., grid cell-like activity; Fig. 4c), providing an abstract structural code that can be used for making inferences in any environment or in new problems that have a similar relational structure. In this way, TEM formalizes how an agent learns representations thought to be present in hippocampal-prefrontal systems. This model allowed us to test whether hippocampal signals more accurately predict the conjunction of concepts and their location in the affective space (activity in layer p), and whether vmPFC signals more accurately predict the relational structure of affective space (activity in layer g).

For TEM agents to experience transitions between emotional events that approximate human experiences, we created an artificial environment based on emotion category ratings provided by participants in the online sample. We discretized the affective space derived from multidimensional scaling (Fig. 3b) into a grid environment (Fig. 4a). During training, agents randomly explored this environment, learning the relational structure of emotion concepts through experience, mimicking one way the brain could learn to represent emotion concepts over time. This simulation enabled us to define representations of emotion concepts and relations between them and evaluate how accurately they can be decoded from patterns of hippocampal activity in the fMRI signal. To model human brain responses during film viewing, we generated TEM activation time series by averaging the activation of layers p and g in artificial agents as they navigated the affective space, weighting the responses in layers p and g using a linear combination of ratings on all emotions at each point. Similar to the multi-scale representations observed in place cells across the hippocampal long axis66,67, TEM includes artificial neurons at multiple levels of abstraction, allowing it to represent both fine-grained and coarse aspects of the environment. Because representations in layers p and g differed the most at small scales in our simulations (Fig. 4c and Supplementary Fig. 15), we predicted that hippocampal decoding of layer p would be more accurate than layer g for units with narrow firing fields (smaller scales), as they better capture transitions between specific emotions as opposed to large transitions in the affective space (larger scales). Consistent with this prediction, we found higher cross-validated decoding performance for layer p than g (Δz = 0.0017, 95% bootstrap CI [0.0001, 0.0034], d = 0.3773, p = 0.015; Fig. 5a). Further, a linear contrast across representational scales revealed that as scale decreased, decoding performance increased more for layer p than for layer g (Δz = 0.0352, 95% bootstrap CI [0.0254, 0.0448], d = 1.3232, p < .001; Fig. 5c), indicating that more accurate decoding of layer p activity was driven by information related to small-scale conjunctive codes.

Because firing field size varies along the hippocampal long axis66,67, we next tested whether information about smaller-scale layer p activity was more strongly represented in the posterior hippocampus. To this end, we trained separate decoding models to predict TEM activations at small (0 and 1) and large representational scales (2 through 4), and compared the accuracy of readouts from anterior versus posterior hippocampal fMRI activity. This analysis revealed differences in decoding accuracy that depended on both hippocampal portion and scale (Δz = 0.0052, 95% bootstrap CI [0.0033, 0.0071], d = 0.9909, p = .002; Fig. 5b, d), indicating that smaller-scale layer p activity was decoded more accurately in posterior than anterior hippocampus.

We observed that hippocampal decoders predicted variation in emotional experience as reflected in both human self-report and the activity of TEM agents. To determine whether decoders utilized common patterns of hippocampal response, we compared decoding performance before and after controlling for predictions of p (see “Methods” ‘Comparing the decoding performance of TEM activity’ for details). We found that accounting for hippocampal signals related to layer p activity impaired the readout of emotion category ratings (Δz = 0.0042, 95% bootstrap CI [0.0020, 0.0061]) more so than trajectories in affective space (Δz = 0.0014, 95% bootstrap CI [0.0000, 0.0029]) and valence-arousal ratings (Δz = 0.0002, 95% bootstrap CI [0.0010, 0.0014]; Δz = 0.0028, 95% bootstrap CI [0.0004, 0.0052], d = 0.4205, p = .003; Δz = 0.0039, 95% bootstrap CI [0.0021, 0.0057], d = 0.7890, p = .001). This result indicates that a conjunctive representation of emotion concepts can account for some, but not all, of the enhanced prediction of emotion category ratings compared to affective dimensions in the hippocampus.

The entorhinal cortex and vmPFC are thought to represent relations among objects, locations, and goal-states in a domain general way36,39,68,69. If these cortical areas play a similar role in representing relations among emotion concepts, decoding layer g activity from these regions should be more accurate than decoding layer p activity. We tested this prediction by comparing the decoding accuracy as a function of brain region (hippocampus, entorhinal cortex, and vmPFC), layer (p and g), and scale (small and large). Analysis of variance revealed that decoding performance depended on all three variables (a three-way interaction: F(8, 616) = 12.44, partial η² = 0.14, p < .001; Supplementary Fig. 16). Direct comparisons (Fig. 5c) indicated that there was better readout of layer g than layer p activity at large scales in vmPFC (Δz = 0.0712, 95% bootstrap CI [0.0614, 0.0809], d = 2.6747, p < .001), and to a lesser degree in the entorhinal cortex (Δz = 0.0099, 95% bootstrap CI [0.0001, 0.0199], d = 0.3680, p = .046). Decoding layer g was more accurate at larger scales in the vmPFC than in both hippocampus (Δz = 0.0542, 95% bootstrap CI [0.0447, 0.0640], d = 2.0455, p < .001; Fig. 5c) and entorhinal cortex (Δz = 0.0604, 95% bootstrap CI [0.0506, 0.0700], d = 2.2580, p < .001; Fig. 5c). Conversely, decoding layer p activity was better at small scales in the hippocampus compared to both entorhinal cortex (Δz = 0.0191, 95% bootstrap CI [0.0093, 0.0289], d = 0.7091, p < .001; Fig. 5c) and vmPFC (Δz = 0.0182, 95% bootstrap CI [0.0086, 0.0279], d = 0.6815, p = .003; Fig. 5c, left and right). Together, these results suggest that the vmPFC contains more information about large-scale structural abstractions (e.g., that one portion of a video was more pleasant than another), whereas the hippocampus represents conjunctive codes of multiple emotion concepts embedded in the affective space.
